episodes.190655: Some strong thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front in an environment with minimal instability and even some capping but strong shear was present.
episodes.190707: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a front in the southern Appalachians and produced significant wind damage as it moved into the northern Midlands from the northwest.
episodes.190722: A front moved through the area as isolated severe storms developed along the front producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.190762: A shortwave trough moving across the Mississippi Valley region sparked thunderstorm development along a pre-existing outflow boundary oriented from northern Mississippi into north central Alabama. During the early evening hours, one particular thunderstorm took advantage of 2500-3000 J/kg of CAPE and 30-40 kt bulk shear values, producing up to 2-inch diameter hail in the Allgood and Oneonta areas of Blount County. This cell also resulted in a few downed trees in Blount and St. Clair counties.
episodes.190835: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms tracked across the South Plains on the evening of the tenth. Storms formed within the vicinity of a remnant mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) from convection from the previous day. A couple of thunderstorms became severe producing both severe wind gusts near Morton (Cochran County) and large hail up to 2.25 inches in diameter in Brownfield (Terry County).
episodes.190860: A strong thunderstorm developed over the water.
episodes.191067: Slow moving thunderstorms produced hail and heavy rainfall as they slowly drift south across the east/southeast part of the Denver Metro area. Additional storms track across Colorado producing hail up to 1 inch in Fairplay and Platteville. Plowable hail occurred under the Fairplay storm.
episodes.191806: A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms over Crook and northern Weston counties developed into a line as it approached the South Dakota border. Hail to around quarter size and wind gusts to 60 mph accompanied the storms.
episodes.191808: Thunderstorms developed across Harding County and eventually formed into a line as they crossed northwest South Dakota. The storms produced some large hail, but mostly wind gusts to over 70 mph across the area.
episodes.191810: Thunderstorms developed along the east slopes of the Black Hills and became severe as they formed into a line east of the Black Hills. This line eventually connected with the line of severe storms across northwest South Dakota as it moved into central South Dakota. The storms produced mostly small hail and wind gusts to over 70 mph across west central into south central South Dakota.
episodes.191813: A severe thunderstorm tracked east-southeast out of Wyoming and across western and southern parts of Fall River County before moving into Nebraska. The storm produced large hail to over golf ball size and wind gusts to 70 mph.
episodes.191817: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over the central Black Hills, producing wind gusts to near 70 mph southeast of Deerfield.
episodes.191870: A small cluster of strong thunderstorms impacted portions of east central and northeastern Carbon County during the early to mid evening hours on 6/9. These storms produced multiple instances of hail between 1 and 2 inches in diameter several miles to the NNE of Medicine Bow.
episodes.191871: Scattered high-based thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts in excess of 60 MPH across portions of south central and southeast Wyoming during the mid to late afternoon hours on 6/10.
episodes.191872: Scattered high-based thunderstorms with a few organized linear clusters spread across the western Nebraska Panhandle from the late afternoon into the early evening hours on 6/10, mainly producing strong wind gusts in excess of 60 MPH in the northern Nebraska Panhandle.
episodes.192071: Storms pushing offshore produced strong wind gusts near Cape Canaveral.
episodes.192519: A low pressure system located across eastern New Mexico brought in an abundance of moisture aloft to the southern and western Texas Panhandle. The high amounts of moisture provided by the low pressure system created a tropical type environment allowing heavy rain showers to develop and move from southeast to northwest across the southern Texas Panhandle. Although the instability was limited, the lift from the low pressure system combined with abnormally high moisture led to rain rates upwards of 1 to 2 inches per hour. These heavy rains fell over an area that had already received over 1 of rainfall earlier in the morning and just over 2 the day before. These rain rates on top of the unique terrain of the canyon contributed to flash flooding that other areas in the Texas Panhandle would otherwise not see. The flash flood conditions caused a few motorists to be stranded and they had to be rescued due to the fast flowing water across some of the roadways. Parts of the canyon had also already received just over 2 the day before and with an additional 4 to 5 by mid afternoon.
episodes.192542: Weak morning coastal showers with a few embedded thunderstorms produce a waterspout offshore of Venice in Sarasota County.
episodes.192566: A line of thunderstorms formed along a stationary front and moved through the western part of South-Central Texas. Some of these storms produced severe wind gusts.
episodes.192599: An organized linear complex of thunderstorms, centered across south-central Kansas, produced a severe-caliber wind gust across far northern Oklahoma during the early morning of the 9th. Additional diurnally-driven convection across southern Oklahoma produced localized flooding and a report of large hail during the evening.
episodes.192980: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon, typical of summertime.  A few trees were blown down in Coffee county with the strongest storms.
episodes.192982: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon, typical of summertime. A few trees were blown down with the strongest storms.
episodes.193194: Storms developed across northeast Mississippi along an outflow boundary generated from earlier convection.  This outflow boundary interacted with an extremely unstable atmosphere. Surface-based convective available potential energy values exceed 4000 J/kg. Storm organization was helped by 0-6km wind shear values that exceeded 30 knots. Several supercells developed with numerous reports of large hail. Some storms split into right and left movers, each producing large hail.
episodes.193420: A strong thunderstorm moved through Lincoln County and brought one inch hail to the western portion of the county. Crop damage was reported the storm. The Weather Service issued a severe storm warning for the storm.
episodes.193427: Mid-level shortwave energy approaching the region along with a nearly stationary cold front across the area provided ample forcing within an environment displaying strong instability, deep moisture, ample shear and very strong downdraft CAPE, leading to strong and severe thunderstorms capable of producing large hail and damaging winds across Southeast Georgia.
episodes.193428: Mid-level shortwave energy approaching the region along with a nearly stationary cold front across the area provided ample forcing within an environment displaying strong instability, deep moisture, ample shear and very strong downdraft CAPE, leading to strong and severe thunderstorms capable of producing large hail and damaging winds across Southeast South Carolina. A notable supercell thunderstorm developed near the Savannah River during the afternoon and tracked northeast through the Tri-County Area during early evening hours, producing a long and wide swath of damaging winds and large hail across inland portions of the Charleston Metro Area.
episodes.193430: Mid-level shortwave energy approaching the region along with a nearly stationary cold front across the area provided ample forcing within an environment displaying strong instability, deep moisture, ample shear and very strong downdraft CAPE, leading to strong and severe thunderstorms capable of producing damaging winds across coastal waters.
episodes.193464: A boundary stalled out over the plains and resulted in the development of strong storms. Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms produced some flash flooding in Huerfano and Pueblo Counties. Isolated stronger storms (sub-severe) also developed further west over Saguache County, resulting in some hail (below severe criteria) and a brief landspout was also reported.
episodes.193465: Snowmelt runoff in the upper Arkansas (above Pueblo) and high flow releases from Pueblo Reservoir resulted in minor flooding at numerous forecast points along the Arkansas River.
episodes.193518: A weak front initiated isolated to scattered thunderstorm in central and south central GA. A few storms became strong to severe with the first strong storms from Troup county over to Putnum county. The line weakened and moved slowly south before redeveloping and strengthening in the far southern CWA. A few storms were able to produce isolated strong wind gusts over 70 mph and some large hail.
episodes.193540: Several reports of severe weather were received through the afternoon.
episodes.193600: A few thunderstorms produced damaging winds in Runnels and Sutton counties and localized flash flooding in Taylor County.
episodes.193635: A large negatively tilted trough to the west of the southern Great Plains and a stalled cold front resulted in numerous afternoon thunderstorms across the region. A few of these thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts.
episodes.193636: A weak, convectively enhanced upper-low over the Texas/New Mexico border aided in the development of severe thunderstorms ahead of this feature. This included hail, damaging winds, and a couple of brief tornadoes.
episodes.193637: A weak, convectively enhanced upper-low over the Texas/New Mexico border aided in the development of severe thunderstorms ahead of this feature. This included hail, damaging winds, and a couple of brief tornadoes.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey Team confirmed straight-line thunderstorm wind damage with an estimated maximum wind speed of 80 to 85 mph along a path approximately 8.75 miles long and 3.5 miles wide beginning in east-central Dorchester County at 642 PM, then tracking across extreme western Charleston County starting at 645 PM, before ending across west-central Berkeley County at 658 PM.||In Dorchester County, the survey team found isolated to scattered damage across areas starting around Bacons Bridge Road to Old Trolley Road, following a general path east-northeast through southern and eastern portions of Summerville. Most of this damage consisted of large softwood trees snapped and uprooted and some hardwood tree limbs snapped. One area of extensive damage occurred around the Quail Arbor Neighborhood off Old Trolley Road, where both soft and hardwood trees were observed to have snapped near the trunks, some of which fell on residences and vehicles. Further east along the path of damage, a Dorchester County emergency manager indicated numerous trees snapped off or blown down within four neighborhoods between Old Trolley Road and Miles Jamison Road. The path of damage then continued into the extreme western portion of Charleston County starting at 645 PM. Based on the uniform damage direction (north to northeast), a strong downburst producing straight-line winds was determined to be the cause of the event.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey Team confirmed straight-line thunderstorm wind damage with an estimated maximum wind speed of 80 to 85 mph along a path approximately 8.75 miles long and 3.5 miles wide beginning in east-central Dorchester County at 642 PM, then tracking across extreme western Charleston County starting at 645 PM, before ending across west-central Berkeley County at 658 PM.||In Berkeley County, the survey team found isolated to scattered damage, most of which consisted of large softwood trees snapped and uprooted and some hardwood tree limbs snapped across eastern portions of Summerville to around Main Street on the north side of Sangaree and south across Ladson and into the College Park area, ending as far east as Highway 176. One area of extensive damage occurred around Wisteria Street and the Tall Pines Neighborhood along Interstate 26 on the north side of Ladson. Within this area, both soft and hardwood trees were observed to have snapped near the trunks, several of which fell on residences and vehicles. Additionally, some minor damage to residential property was observed, including shingles and siding blown off and privacy fences blown down. The path of damage continued east-northeastward from the Tall Pines Neighborhood where a tree was reported down on a vehicle along with damage to a fence and siding in the Hunter's Bend Neighborhood before the path of damage continued across much of the College Park area. A Berkeley County emergency manager indicated at least 28 homes damaged by falling trees in the College Park vicinity and a pole barn significantly damaged along Cindy Drive. One female was reported injured when a tree fell on her residence on College Park Drive. Emergency management also reported at least 18 additional downed trees and power lines in the area not directly impacting homes. The damage path then continued east-northward across Fairfax and Oakbrook Neighborhoods where a Berkeley County emergency manager indicated numerous trees down on roadways, homes and cars, before the damage path ended near Highway 176 at 658 PM. Based on the uniform damage direction (north to northeast), a strong downburst producing straight-line winds was determined to be the cause of the event.
